query: For a FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy used as a thin coating on a conventional metal substrate, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs overall wear resistance and microscopic deformation during sliding in the intended high-temperature operating regime? Define a controlled change relative to a baseline coating condition, predict the corresponding directional changes in wear and deformation, state the regime in which those predictions should hold, identify supporting prior evidence, and specify a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a post-deposition rapid thermal annealing step that refines the near-surface grain structure of the FeNiCrCoCu coating will promote the formation of an ultra-nanocrystalline, self-strengthening tribolayer during high-temperature sliding, thereby reducing localized shear (serrated plastic deformation) and lowering wear loss compared to the untreated (coarse-grained) baseline.
generation.material_initial_state: As-deposited FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy coating with a relatively coarse near-surface grain structure on a conventional metal substrate.
generation.intervention: Apply a rapid thermal annealing process immediately after deposition to induce significant grain refinement near the surface.
generation.conditions: High-temperature sliding wear tests, simulating the intended operating regime (elevated temperatures where dynamic recovery/recrystallization are active).
generation.structural_mediator: Refined near-surface grain structure that facilitates the in situ formation of a hard, ultra-nanocrystalline tribolayer.
generation.mechanism: The thermal treatment activates dynamic recrystallization in the near-surface region of the coating, reducing the grain size. This refined structure promotes the development of a cohesive tribolayer under sliding conditions, which in turn suppresses localized shear banding and abrupt slip events (serrations), leading to more homogeneous microscopic deformation and enhanced wear resistance.
generation.predicted_outcome: The thermally treated coating will exhibit lower friction coefficients and reduced wear volume during high-temperature sliding, with smoother stress-strain behavior (fewer or smaller stress drops) compared to the baseline coating.
generation.baseline: Coating without the additional rapid thermal annealing step, having a coarser near-surface grain structure and lacking a well-developed self-forming tribolayer.
generation.boundary: The predicted improvements are expected within the high-temperature regime where dynamic recrystallization and tribolayer formation are feasible; at extremely high temperatures or in regimes with excessive thermal softening, the effects may differ.
generation.uncertainty: While literature on similar HEA systems and wear-resistant coatings supports the beneficial role of refined grain structures and tribofilm formation, the precise optimal annealing parameters (temperature, duration) and exact grain size threshold for maximizing the effect in FeNiCrCoCu coatings remain to be established.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of identical FeNiCrCoCu coatings on the same metal substrate. One set receives the rapid thermal annealing treatment (intervention) and the other remains as-deposited (baseline). Subject both sets to identical high-temperature sliding wear tests.
measurements: Surface microstructure analysis (grain size distribution and tribolayer characterization via SEM/TEM)
Stress-strain behavior during sliding to detect serrations
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis will be falsified if the thermally treated coatings do not exhibit statistically significant improvements in wear resistance (lower wear volume and smoother stress-strain curves) or if no refined near-surface tribolayer is observed compared to the untreated baseline.

cited_evidence.text: A series of new tensile deformation experiments is presented, which are performed at slow strain-rates on metals ranging from conventional alloys (i.e., with fewer than five principal elements) to high-entropy alloys (HEAs). HEAs are new alloys that contain at least five principal elements of roughly-equal proportion. They are high-performance materials with excellent properties for elevated-temperature applications, such as boilers and turbines. In a certain temperature and strain-rate regime, HEAs deform via sudden slips that are visible as stress drops or “serrations” in the stress-strain curves. These slips can make it difficult to precisely control the deformation behavior. Understanding how their sizes can be reduced could be used to smoothen the deformation properties, and, thus, make the deformation process more predictable and easier to control.

The AlCoCrFeNiSi HEA coating showed a volume wear rate of (0.38 ± 0.08) × 10−4 mm3·N−1·m−1, which is about half that of the AlCoCrFeNiTi coating in our previous study (0.77 ± 0.01) × 10−4 mm3·N−1·m−1 [] at the same test conditions. This result indicates that the wear resistance of the AlCoCrFeNiSi coating was better than that of the AlCoCrFeNiTi coating. Besides, comparing with the conventional flame-sprayed NiCrBSi coating with a volume wear rate of about 1.7 × 10−4 mm3·N−1·m−1 [], the coating in this paper also showed much better wear resistance. All of these results make the APS AlCoCrFeNiSi coating a promising one that can be used in abrasion environments in the industries of petroleum, power, mining, and so on. Besides the high density of the coating and the high hardness of the AlCoCrFeNiSi material, formation of the hard tribofilms (Figure 13) can be another reason for the good wear resistance.

An Al0.5CoCrCuFeNi high-entropy alloy coating was successfully fabricated on an AZ91D matrix by laser cladding using mixed powders of Cu, Ni, Al, Co, Cr, and Fe. The Al0.5CoCrCuFeNi high-entropy alloy coating consisted of fine dendrites with a simple FCC phase. The dry sliding wear resistance of the Al0.5CoCrCuFeNi high-entropy alloy coating prepared by laser cladding was better than that of the AZ91D matrix, and the wear mechanisms of the two materials were different. The Al0.5CoCrCuFeNi high-entropy alloy coating prepared by laser cladding had better corrosion resistance than did the AZ91D matrix in 3.5 wt % sodium chloride solution.
